Twilight
TWY-lite
noun
From twi-, two or between (as in twice, twain), and light: the between-light, the doubtful glimmer at either end of the day. It renders the Hebrew nesheph, which serves for both the dusk and the dawn — the hour when the eye can no longer tell.

Biblical Definition

Twilight is the doubtful light at the edges of the day, and Scripture almost always sets a man moving in it. It is first the hour of the sinner who wants a witness and cannot bear one: “The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight, saying, No eye shall see me: and disguiseth his face” (Job 24:15). He does not choose the black of midnight, which would be suspicious, but the half-light, where a face is a smudge; and Job’s indictment is that the man reckons on an eye that cannot see, having forgotten the eye that never closes. Solomon sets the young man void of understanding in the same hour, going toward the strange woman’s corner “in the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night” (Pro 7:9) — and note that the twilight slides into blackness before the paragraph ends, which is how sin always keeps its appointments. But twilight is also the hour of God’s deliverances. The four lepers rose in the twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians and found it empty (2Ki 7:5), because the LORD had made the host to hear a noise of chariots and they “fled in the twilight” (2Ki 7:7), leaving their tents and their horses and their food to feed a starving city. Ezekiel is commanded to dig through the wall and carry out his stuff in the twilight as a sign to a house that would not see (Eze 12:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

The faint light before sunrise and after sunset; hence any dubious or uncertain half-light, in which the eye cannot rightly judge.

expand to see more

TWILIGHT, n. [twi, two or between, and light.] The faint light which is reflected before sunrise and after sunset; the light of the dusk and of the dawn.

Dubious or uncertain view; faint and doubtful knowledge; as the twilight of the understanding.

adj. Obscure; imperfectly illuminated; seen dimly.

The hour of the adulterer’s disguise (Job 24:15) and of the young man’s ruin (Pro 7:9).

Also the hour of the Syrians’ flight and Samaria’s deliverance (2Ki 7:5, 7).

Key Scripture

Job 24:15 — "The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight, saying, No eye shall see me: and disguiseth his face."

2Ki 7:5 — "And they rose up in the twilight, to go unto the camp of the Syrians: and when they were come to the uttermost part of the camp of Syria, behold, there was no man there."

2Ki 7:7 — "Wherefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, and their horses, and their asses, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life."

Eze 12:6 — "In their sight shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulders, and carry it forth in the twilight: thou shalt cover thy face, that thou see not the ground: for I have set thee for a sign unto the house of Israel."

Modern Corruption

The half-light is treated as a place where God does not look — the private hour, the anonymous screen, the sin no one can name — against Scripture’s testimony that the darkness and the light are both alike to Him.

expand to see more

Job’s adulterer has multiplied beyond counting, and the twilight he waits for is now electric. The half-light is the private browser, the deleted thread, the second account, the hotel in another city, the disguised face of an anonymous handle — every arrangement built on the calculation Job puts in the man’s own mouth: No eye shall see me. The calculation is false at the root, and Scripture answers it without pity or exaggeration: the eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good; the darkness hideth not from Him, but the night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are both alike to Him (Psa 139:12); and there is no creature that is not manifest in His sight, all things being naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13). The twilight sinner is not hidden. He is merely unobserved by men for a season, which is not the same thing, and God has appointed a day when the hidden things of darkness shall be brought to light and the counsels of the hearts made manifest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that twilight is God’s hour too, and that He works most often exactly where men can see least. The four lepers rose in the twilight with nothing but the logic of desperation — if we sit still here, we die — and walked into an abandoned camp, because the LORD had already emptied it with a noise no human army made. Samaria was fed that night, and the sneering lord who said it could not be done saw it with his eyes and did not eat thereof. Ezekiel carried his stuff out in the twilight as a sign to a rebellious house. The doubtful light is where faith actually walks: not in noonday certainty but in the half-light, on the word of God alone, one step at a time. Children of the day do not lurk in the dusk to sin; they cross it to obey.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Twi- (between) + light: the between-light; Hebrew nesheph, serving for both dusk and dawn.

expand to see more

Twilight — twi-, two or between (cf. twain, twice) + light.

Hebrew nesheph (H5399) — used of both the evening dusk and the morning glimmer.

Job 24:15 and Pro 7:9 give the sinner’s twilight; 2Ki 7:5, 7 give the LORD’s.

Pro 7:9 stacks the hours — twilight, evening, black and dark night — the slide of sin.

Eze 12:6 makes the twilight removal a prophetic sign to a blind house.

Usage

"The adulterer chooses twilight, not midnight — enough light to move, too little to be known."

"“No eye shall see me” is the twilight creed, and Psa 139:12 is its answer."

"The lepers rose in the twilight and found the camp empty: God works in the half-light too."
